questions.question: 1. Large-scale propagation models, which include pathloss and shadowing, are used to predict what?

answers.a: The average signal strength over long distances.
answers.b: Instantaneous signal changes due to device movement.
answers.c: The data throughput of a wireless link.
answers.d: The battery life of a mobile device.

questions.question: 2. What is the primary difference between large-scale fading and small-scale fading?

answers.a: Large-scale fading happens indoors; small-scale fading happens outdoors.
answers.b: Large-scale fading involves distance and obstructions; small-scale fading involves rapid fluctuations from multi-path.
answers.c: Large-scale fading only affects high frequencies; small-scale fading only affects low frequencies.
answers.d: There is no difference; they are two terms for the same effect.

questions.question: 3. The pathloss exponent in a perfect free-space environment, with no obstructions or reflections, is exactly...?
4. When determining the pathloss exponent from measurements, what is the standard graphical method?

answers.a: Plotting received power versus distance on a linear scale and finding the curve.
answers.b: Finding the slope of the best-fit line on a plot of signal power (in dB) versus the logarithm of distance.
answers.c: Counting the number of buildings in the signal path.
answers.d: Measuring the transmitter's exact power output at the antenna.

questions.question: 5. Shadow fading is considered a 'random' process because...?

answers.a: ...the signal strength changes completely unpredictably from one second to the next.
answers.b: ...it is impossible to know the transmitter's location.
answers.c: ...the exact size, shape, and location of obstructions are complex and vary from one path to another.
answers.d: ...it is caused by random noise from the sun.

questions.question: 6. What would a shadow fading variance of zero practically imply?

answers.a: The signal is perfectly blocked at all times.
answers.b: All signal measurements at a given distance are exactly the same as the average predicted by the pathloss model.
answers.c: The environment is extremely cluttered and complex.
answers.d: The pathloss exponent must also be zero.

questions.question: 7. To properly analyze the statistical characteristics of shadowing, what must be done to the raw signal measurements?

answers.a: The predictable signal loss due to distance (pathloss) must be subtracted out first.
answers.b: Only the strongest signal measurement should be kept for analysis.
answers.c: Only the weakest signal measurement should be kept for analysis.
answers.d: All measurements must be averaged into a single number for the entire area.

questions.question: 8. What is a 'propagation model' in the context of wireless communications?

answers.a: A physical antenna used to send signals.
answers.b: A set of rules for how to speak on a mobile phone.
answers.c: A mathematical description used to characterize signal behavior from transmitter to receiver.
answers.d: A software program that blocks unwanted signals.

questions.question: 9. A measured pathloss exponent of 2.5 suggests the environment is...?

answers.b: ...slightly more obstructed than free space, or includes some reflections.
answers.c: ...a very dense city with many tall buildings.

questions.question: 10. Why is understanding shadow fading variance crucial for wireless network planning?

answers.a: It helps determine the exact data speed a single user will get at a specific moment.
answers.b: It is not crucial and is usually ignored in favor of pathloss.
answers.c: It helps predict the reliability of signal coverage, allowing planners to design for a certain percentage of users.
answers.d: It tells the network planner what brand of antenna to purchase.
